items.title: Co-production using Theory of Change in the development of the SUCCEED Africa community-based rehabilitation intervention for people living with psychosis in West and Southeast Africa
items.authors: Julian Eaton, Olubukola Christianah Omobowale, Rita Frinue Tamambang, Rachel Greenley
items.abstract: Psychosis and other severe mental health conditions cause substantial disability and reduced functioning across a number of domains. Services in low- and middle-income settings are often weak, and predominantly biomedical. Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR) offers a comprehensive and person-centred approach that is aligned to effective case management models. The Support, Comprehensive Care and Empowerment for People with Psychosocial Disabilities (SUCCEED) programme was co-produced with people living with psychosis in four sub-Saharan countries, with a view to improving quality of life, mental health outcomes, and community participation. This paper described the intervention development process, using multiple iterations of Theory of Change (ToC), incorporating situation analysis, formative research and piloting. We present these iterations as results, using the GUIDED framework for intervention development, and the intervention is described using the TIDieR framework. We conclude that ToC can promote participatory processes of intervention co-development, as well as generate research questions. Interventions must remain flexible, and be open to revision, even if having core active ingredients.

items.title: Calling All Restroom Revolutionaries!
items.authors: Simone Chess, Alison Kafer, Jessi Quizar, Mattie Udora Richardson
items.abstract: Everyone needs to use bathrooms, but only some of us have to enter into complicated political and architectural negotiations in order to use them. The fact is, bathrooms are easier to access for some of us than for others, and the people who never think about where and how they can pee have a lot of control over how using restrooms feels for the rest of us. What do we need from bathrooms? What elements are necessary to make a bathroom functional for everyone? To make it safe? To make it a private and respectful space? Whose bodies are excluded from the typical restroom? More important, what kind of bodies are assumed in the design of these bathrooms? Who has the privilege (we call it pee-privilege) of never needing to think about these issues, of always knowing that any given bathroom will meet one’s needs? Everyone needs to use the bathroom. But not all of us can.

items.title: Integrating Disability, Transforming Feminist Theory
items.abstract: My title here, “Integrating Disability, Transforming Feminist Theory,” invokes and links two notions, integration and transformation, both of which are fundamental to the feminist project and to the larger Civil Rights Movement that informed it. Integration suggests achieving parity by fully including that which has been excluded and subordinated. Transformation suggests re-imagining established knowledge and the order of things. By alluding to integration and transformation, I set my own modest project of integrating disability into feminist theory in the politicized context of the Civil Rights Movement in order to gesture toward the explicit relation that feminism supposes between intellectual work and a commitment to creating a more just, equitable, and integrated society.

items.title: The Academic Origins of Disability Studies and the Society for Disability Studies
items.authors: Rosemarie Garland‐Thomson, Rannveig Traustadóttir, Nirmala Erevelles
items.abstract: Based on a conversation with Rosemarie Garland-Thomson, this chapter examines the scholarly and academic labor involved in the emergence of critical disability studies in the United States, with particular attention to efforts to foreground disability culture, access, and justice across a wide range of institutions and communities. It explores how disability studies has critically interrogated cultural representations of disability and how, especially within the humanities, the field has reframed disability as a minority discourse rather than a medical problem. Through this shift, critical disability studies has challenged oppressive narratives and made visible more liberatory ways of understanding disability. Central to this account is the leadership and influence of Steve Taylor, whose vision and work were instrumental in shaping the field’s intellectual foundations and ethical commitments.

items.title: The Color of Violence
items.abstract: As I write this chapter, I am very conscious I am writing in a time of war. Almost daily there are reports of roadside bombs detonating; the launching of military offensives; power failures; and shortages of food, drinking water, and fuel in the “postwar” contexts of a devastated Afghanistan and an occupied Iraq. Not much has changed since President Obama announced the complete pull-out of U.S. troops from Iraq and Afghanistan in the near future. Here, in the United States, a few news media organizations keep diligent count of U.S. soldiers killed in the war. Even more infrequently, and almost always as a passing note, we hear a rare report of disabled war veterans returning from combat. While there are some reports of civilian deaths in Afghanistan and Iraq, I have been unable to find reports of Afghan and Iraqi civilians and members of the military (and now the insurgency) who have become disabled as a result of the war and the postwar conflict. I find this extremely troubling, but neither the alternative press nor radical scholars in the academy seem perturbed by these omissions.

items.title: Introduction
items.authors: Rannveig Traustadóttir, Nirmala Erevelles, Zana Marie Lutfiyya, Rachael A. Zubal-Ruggieri
items.abstract: In June 2023, a group of international scholars and former doctoral graduates of Syracuse University gathered for a reunion to reflect on their years as students and colleagues. As they shared memories of their intellectual journeys, one theme emerged with remarkable clarity and unanimity: the professor who had most profoundly shaped their thinking, their values, and their aspirations as scholars was Professor Steven J. Taylor. Many confessed that, throughout their careers, they had quietly measured themselves against the kind of academic Steve Taylor was – and they hoped to become. Steven J. Taylor (1949–2014) was a humble giant in disability studies. Reluctant to seek the limelight, he nonetheless exerted an immense and enduring influence on the field. His scholarship was instrumental in reconceptualizing disability as a socially constructed category of difference, challenging medicalized and deficit-based understandings that had long dominated research, policy, and practice. Yet Steve was never a detached academic. He believed deeply that research and scholarship must matter – that they must make a tangible difference in the lives of disabled people and contribute to social change, justice, and human dignity.

items.title: Belonging, Dignity, and Justice
items.authors: Rannveig Traustadóttir, Zana Marie Lutfiyya, Nirmala Erevelles
items.abstract: The book’s concluding chapter brings together personal and scholarly reflections on the legacy of Steven J. Taylor, offered by disability studies scholars and advocates who have not contributed to earlier sections of the book. These accounts situate Taylor’s influence within the international development of disability studies. The contributions reflect on the distinctive role of Syracuse University and the Center on Human Policy as an intellectual and moral home where disability studies was practiced, integrating scholarship, advocacy, and community life. Collectively, the reflections highlight how Taylor’s work reshaped understandings of disability as socially produced, relational, and fundamentally tied to questions of dignity, belonging, and human rights. Contributors emphasize Taylor’s enduring influence through mentorship, collaboration, and the formation of scholars and advocates across disciplines and national contexts, illustrating how his work generated ripples that continue to shape disability studies globally. The chapter concludes by identifying future directions for the field, including renewed attention to institutionalization and resistance to the contemporary backlash against disability rights. In doing so, it affirms that Steve Taylor’s legacy endures not only in texts and institutions, but also in the values and practices that continue to guide disability studies as a project of justice, inclusion, and collective responsibility.

items.title: Rethinking Community as Praxis
items.abstract: Through a reflective conversation, we – Nirmala Erevelles and Susan Burch – as disability studies scholars draw on our different disciplinary backgrounds to identify connections to Steve Taylor and his work. Centering on Steve Taylor’s scholarship about intellectual disability, particularly through his concept of a sociology of acceptance, Erevelles theorizes disability in ranging contexts – historical, contemporary, American, and the Global South. Burch’s work on the history of deaf people and institutionalization identifies relationships and locations that overlap with, and move beyond, Steve Taylor’s research. An emphasis on relational analyses provides a launching-off point for further theorization and historicization. Pondering the implications of Taylor’s work on our field(s), we trace the ways our scholarship builds on, and at other times critiques, his work. Telescoping out, we identify arguments to meet some of the theoretical and methodological challenges that mark our field. Collectively marking the continuities and discontinuities from Steve Taylor’s scholarship and our own, we return to the beginning, reimagining community as a form of praxis.
